hints: Focus on the three factors that control ionisation energy: nuclear charge, distance of the outer electron, and shielding.
Compare the nuclei, K has 19 protons with electron configuration $\text{[Ar] 4s}^1$ while Sr has 38 protons with configuration $\text{[Kr] 5s}^2$.
Ask yourself which factor acts to pull the outer electron more strongly and so would increase the energy needed to remove it.
walkthrough:
**Recall what first ionisation energy depends on**

First ionisation energy is the energy needed to remove one outer electron. It increases with greater nuclear charge, and decreases with greater distance and greater shielding.

$$\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^+\text{(g)} + \text{e}^-$$

**Compare the atoms of K and Sr**

Potassium is $\text{[Ar] 4s}^1$ with nuclear charge +19. Strontium is $\text{[Kr] 5s}^2$ with nuclear charge +38.

So Sr has a much larger nuclear charge, but its outer $\text{5s}$ electron is further out and is shielded by more inner shells.

**Decide which factor explains the higher value**

Distance and extra shielding alone would lower the ionisation energy of Sr. The only factor working in the opposite direction is the much greater proton number.

Since Sr actually has the higher first ionisation energy ($548$ vs $418$ kJ mol-1), the large increase in nuclear charge must outweigh the other effects.

options.A: Correct. Nuclear charge rises from +19 in K to +38 in Sr. This much stronger attraction for the outer electron outweighs the extra distance and shielding, so more energy is needed to remove the electron from Sr.
options.B: Incorrect. Sr does have more inner electrons so shielding is greater, but greater shielding weakens attraction and would lower ionisation energy, not raise it. This would predict K > Sr, the opposite of what is observed.
options.C: Incorrect. The Sr outer shell is $\text{5s}^2$, so the two electrons are paired, but spin-pair repulsion makes an electron easier to remove and lowers ionisation energy. It cannot explain why Sr has a higher value than K which has an unpaired $\text{4s}^1$ electron.
options.D: Incorrect. The Sr $\text{5s}$ electron is in a higher principal quantum shell than the K $\text{4s}$ electron, so it is further away. Greater distance weakens attraction and would lower ionisation energy, not increase it.
